entities.summary:
Telecles, a Hellenistic philosopher likely originating from Phocis or Phocaea, served as a prominent scholarch (head) of Plato's Academy in Athens during the mid-3rd to mid-2nd centuries BCE, specifically co-leading it after 206 BCE until his death in 166 BCE. His tenure marked a critical transitional phase within the Middle Academy, characterized by its skeptical leanings and a unique shift in leadership structure following the death of Lacydes of Cyrene. His role as joint head with Evander of Phocis underscores a distinctive period of shared intellectual authority in this foundational philosophical institution, maintaining its influence amidst the vibrant intellectual landscape of Hellenistic Greece.

Telecles assumed the position of scholarch alongside Evander, a notable departure from the traditional singular leadership model, after Lacydes, who had led the Academy from 241 BCE, retired due to illness around 206 BCE. This dual leadership continued until Telecles' death in 166 BCE, after which Evander remained the sole scholarch for a brief period. Although no specific writings or distinct doctrines of Telecles survive independently, his significance lies in his participation in sustaining the skeptical tradition inaugurated by Arcesilaus and continued by Lacydes, influencing students through oral instruction and dialectical debate within the Academy's venerable walls. This period saw a refinement of Academic skepticism, challenging dogmatic assertions and emphasizing the suspension of judgment (epochē).
